--- title: "DESEq2 workflow" description: "Differential expression analysis of bulk RNA-seq data with DESeq2, using the airway dataset." author: Wiktor Mikolajczak output: html_document: df_print: paged editor_options: chunk_output_type: inline --- # Note Use this vignette as a general guideline, not a ground truth. There is no one way to analyze genomics data. Sometimes you have to adjust your analysis based on your research question, experimental design etc. In the future you will analyze genomic data that you or other people generated. It is vital that, before any analysis, you familiarize yourself with the data set: - What is the biological question you are trying to answer? What are the hypotheses? - What is the study design and how was the experiment done (sample type, treatment, genetic knockout, disease, sample size, system, are there any batches etc.)? - How was the data processed (software, genome version etc.)? - What type of data are available (raw data, count matrix, sample metadata)? Instead of just copy-pasting the code, try implementing the following logic: 1. Read the vignette first. Try to understand each step. 2. Without looking at the vignette, write down the main steps of the workflow (use headers to build an outline of your document at the same time). For each step, write a short comment: What is this step for?, Why is it important? Compare your answers with the vignette. It is ok if you don't remember the exact code or the name of the functions. It's more important that you understand each step conceptually. 3. After each step write down your observations. What has changed? Why did you choose this DESeq design? How does PCA explain the data? Are there any batch/technical effects? How many DEGs? etc. 4. At the end of your analysis, think about and write down conclusions. It doesn't have to be an academic assay but try to state the main points and do a little bit of goggling. - Are you able to answer the initial research question and confirm/deny the hypotheses? - Try to connect what is known with what you have found. If you have any questions, check the [DESEq2 vignette](https://bioconductor.org/packages/devel/bioc/vignettes/DESeq2/inst/doc/DESeq2.html). The goal of this training is to help you understand the general workflow of differential gene expression analysis. Although using AI can be beneficial and speed up your analysis, it is important that you have a good understanding of topics covered in this training and you have truly mastered the skill. Only then you can use AI to help you with the analysis. It is fine, to ask AI to help you with customizing a ggplot, but try not to use it for the actual analysis. If you don't know what a function does, run `?function_name` in Console. # About the dataset This workflow uses the **airway** dataset (Bioconductor package `airway`), an RNA-seq experiment from [Himes et al. 2014, *PLoS ONE*](https://doi.org/10.1371/journal.pone.0099625) (GEO: [GSE52778](https://www.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/geo/query/acc.cgi?acc=GSE52778)). The code used to generate the tables can be found [data/airway/airway_generate_counts.R](https://github.com/wiktormiko/Intro-to-genomics/blob/main/vignettes/data/airway/airway_generate_counts.R) The count matrix and sample sheet can be found [here](https://github.com/wiktormiko/Intro-to-genomics/tree/main/vignettes/data/airway). - **Biological question:** how do human airway smooth muscle (ASM) cells respond to dexamethasone, a glucocorticoid used to treat asthma and inflammation? - **Design:** four ASM cell lines (`N61311`, `N052611`, `N080611`, `N061011`), each either left untreated (`untrt`) or treated with dexamethasone (`trt`). - **Size:** 8 samples (4 cell lines x 2 conditions) and 63,677 genes. - **Count matrix** (`airway_raw_counts.csv`): rows are genes (Ensembl IDs), columns are samples (SRA run IDs, e.g. `SRR1039508`). Values are raw, unnormalized read counts. - **Metadata** (`airway_metadata.csv`): one row per sample. - `cell`: the cell line. - `dex`: dexamethasone treatment (`trt` / `untrt`). This is the main variable of interest. - `albut`: albuterol treatment. Every sample here is `untrt`, so it carries no information. - `SampleName`, `Run`, `Experiment`, `Sample`, `BioSample`: GEO / SRA identifiers. - `avgLength`: average read length. Full description: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # library(airway) # vignette("airway") ``` ::: Because each cell line appears in both conditions, the design is **paired**. In the DESeq2 model, `cell` should be included as a covariate alongside `dex`. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} library(tidyverse) library(DESeq2) library(annotables) library(PCAtools) library(EnhancedVolcano) library(clusterProfiler) ``` ::: # Import the data ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_counts <- read.csv("data/airway/airway_raw_counts.csv", row.names = 1) mtd <- read.csv("data/airway/airway_metadata.csv", row.names = 1) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(raw_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Count matrix is a table where rows correspond to gene names and columns - to samples. The gene names are encoded in "ENSEMBL" system. We will convert those names to SYMBOLs - regular gene names. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(mtd) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: Metadata contains information about samples. Each row is a sample and each column describes a metric. For example, we can put information about treatment, batch, collection date, patient ID, etc. This is a publicly available dataset and the metadata info is shared. If you perform the experiment yourself, it is important to create such table yourself with as many details about a sample as you can. It is important that the count table and metadata are matching. Column names of the count matrix and row names of the metadata have to be the same! We can ensure those two are matching by running this: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} all(rownames(mtd) == colnames(raw_counts)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] TRUE ``` ::: ::: if they're not in the right order we can use `match()` to reorder one table so it lines up with the other: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_counts <- raw_counts[, match(rownames(mtd), colnames(raw_counts))] ``` ::: # Pre–filtering ## Remove low count genes It is not necessary to filter out low count genes, because DESEq pipeline does it automatically (`independent filtering`), but applying a small cutoff might make the object smaller and require less computational power and memory. This cutoff is taken from the vignette. It's also common to use `filterByExp` from edgeR package `smallestGroupSize` - we have 4 treated and 4 controls so we will use 4. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} table(mtd$dex) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` trt untrt 4 4 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ngenes_before <- nrow(raw_counts) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} smallestGroupSize <- 4 keep <- rowSums(raw_counts >= 10) >= smallestGroupSize raw_counts <- raw_counts[keep,] ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} ngenes_after <- nrow(raw_counts) cat("#genes before filtering: ", ngenes_before, "\n #genes after filtering: ", ngenes_after) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` #genes before filtering: 63677 #genes after filtering: 16139 ``` ::: ::: 1. `raw_counts >= 10` gives a table of TRUE/FALSE with the same shape as the counts. Each cell asks whether this gene had at least 10 reads in this sample. 2. `rowSums(...)` adds up the TRUE values for each gene, giving the number of samples where the gene reached 10 reads. 3. `>= smallestGroupSize` asks whether that number is at least the size of your smallest experimental group. A gene that is truly different between conditions should have decent counts in all the samples of at least one group. If your smallest group has 4 samples, requiring at least 4 samples with 10 or more reads means a gene could pass by being expressed in just one condition, such as a gene that is switched on only after treatment. A gene with high counts in only 1 of 8 samples is most likely noise or an outlier, so it is dropped. ## Convert ENSEMBL to SYMBOL Before we do any analysis, we need to do a little bit of a cleanup. First we need to convert the ENS to SYMBOL. We will use `annotables` package, that provides per gene information for different genome versions. `airway` dataset uses Grch37 genome assembly. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(grch37) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: We will use this table to build our own gene annotation table. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_anno <- data.frame(ensgene = rownames(raw_counts)) %>% left_join(grch37, by= "ensgene") %>% distinct(symbol, .keep_all = TRUE) %>% # sometimes one ENSEMBL might have two different SYMBOLs or ENTREZ. It might happen where there are multiple isoforms of one gene etc. This makes sure that when an ENS is doubled, we only take the first observation. rename(gene_start = start, gene_end = end, gene_strand = strand) # start/end/strand are reserved names in rowData (GRanges), so DESeq2 would error ``` ::: ## Retain only protein coding genes As you can see there are more than 60,000 genes in our dataset (before filtering). Human genome has around 20,000 genes, so how is it possible? Let's investigate `biotype` column ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} table(gene_anno$biotype) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` 3prime_overlapping_ncRNA antisense lincRNA 1 635 662 miRNA misc_RNA Mt_rRNA 13 13 2 Mt_tRNA polymorphic_pseudogene processed_transcript 3 10 141 protein_coding pseudogene rRNA 13055 1461 3 sense_intronic sense_overlapping snoRNA 64 53 4 snRNA TR_C_gene 1 1 ``` ::: ::: A lot of the transcripts are not even protein coding genes. Lots of them are non-coding RNA, rRNA etc. In this analysis we only care about protein coding genes. First we will subset `gene_anno` to only **protein coding genes** and use that table to subset. We will also remove **mitochondrial genes**, since in our analysis we are not focusing on them. Depending on how the library prep was done, some protocols enrich for poly-A molecule, which should remove mitochondrial RNA. In this case any left over mito genes are just "pollution". It is very easy to identify mitochondrial genes - they have a prefix MT- (human) or mt- (mouse). If we are not sure whether we should remove mito genes, go back to the experimental design and research question. We can calculate a per-sample mitochondrial genes percentage if necessary. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} gene_anno <- gene_anno %>% filter(biotype == 'protein_coding') %>% filter(!grepl("^MT-", symbol, ignore.case = TRUE)) # remove mitochondrial genes (MT- human, mt- mouse) dim(gene_anno) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13042 9 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} raw_counts <- raw_counts[gene_anno$ensgene, ] # retain only protein coding genes rownames(raw_counts) <- gene_anno$symbol # replace ENS with symbols count table rownames(gene_anno) <- gene_anno$symbol ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dim(raw_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 13042 8 ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(raw_counts) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} `````{=html}
````` ::: ::: We are left with \~13,000 genes # DESeq2 workflow: Part I We prepared the metadata and count matrix. We are ready to create a deseq object (`dds`). IT IS IMPORTANT THAT THE COUNTS ARE RAW! If the counts are integers, they are most likely raw counts. ## Design The **design** is a formula that tells DESeq2 which factors may explain differences in gene expression between your samples. It is written as `~ variable1 + variable2`, where each variable is a column name from the metadata table - just like linear regression. **Why is it important?** DESeq2 fits a model for every gene using the design. It uses that model to separate the effect you care about (here, the drug) from other sources of variation (here, the cell line). If the design is wrong or incomplete, the variation you did not account for stays in the noise. That can hide real differences or create false ones. The design cannot be fixed after the fact without re-running the analysis, so it is worth getting right before you create `dds`. **How do we decide what goes there?** 1. Start from your biological question. We want to know which genes change with dexamethasone, so `dex` goes in. 2. Add the other variables that are known to affect expression and that you want to correct for, such as cell line, batch, sex, or age. Here the same four cell lines appear both treated and untreated, and different cell lines naturally express genes differently, so `cell` goes in. This is called paired design. 3. Put the variable of interest **last**. DESeq2 tests the last variable in the formula by default. 4. Only use columns that exist in the metadata, and only the ones that matter. Identifiers (sample name, run ID) are different for every sample and must not go in the design. Variables that are constant (like `albut` here) carry no information. Don't add variables just because you have them, since each one uses up samples that could have gone into the real comparison. So our design is `~ cell + dex`. In plain words: "compare treated and untreated samples, but control for individual effects of each cell line"). **Paired design:** the same cell line (or patient, animal, etc.) is measured in both conditions, so every treated sample has an untreated "partner". **Why control for it?** Cell lines differ from each other far more than we expect treatment to change a typical gene. If `cell` is not in the design, that cell-to-cell variation lands in the noise, so real drug effects are harder to detect. With `cell` in the design, we account for these cell-line specific effects, focusing on the drug effect. ## Create a DESeq object Let's relevel the factors in `dex` column to make sure that untrt is the reference. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} mtd$dex <- factor(mtd$dex, levels = c('untrt', 'trt')) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds <- DESeqDataSetFromMatrix(countData = raw_counts, colData = mtd, rowData = gene_anno, design = ~ cell + dex) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class: DESeqDataSet dim: 13042 8 metadata(1): version assays(1): counts rownames(13042): TSPAN6 DPM1 ... GTF2H5 NUDT3 rowData names(9): ensgene entrez ... biotype description colnames(8): SRR1039508 SRR1039509 ... SRR1039520 SRR1039521 colData names(9): SampleName cell ... Sample BioSample ``` ::: ::: dds object contains all this individual information and tables in one object. Each element can be accessed ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds@design ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` ~cell + dex ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(dds@colData) # metadata ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DataFrame with 6 rows and 9 columns SampleName cell dex albut Run avgLength SRR1039508 GSM1275862 N61311 untrt untrt SRR1039508 126 SRR1039509 GSM1275863 N61311 trt untrt SRR1039509 126 SRR1039512 GSM1275866 N052611 untrt untrt SRR1039512 126 SRR1039513 GSM1275867 N052611 trt untrt SRR1039513 87 SRR1039516 GSM1275870 N080611 untrt untrt SRR1039516 120 SRR1039517 GSM1275871 N080611 trt untrt SRR1039517 126 Experiment Sample BioSample SRR1039508 SRX384345 SRS508568 SAMN02422669 SRR1039509 SRX384346 SRS508567 SAMN02422675 SRR1039512 SRX384349 SRS508571 SAMN02422678 SRR1039513 SRX384350 SRS508572 SAMN02422670 SRR1039516 SRX384353 SRS508575 SAMN02422682 SRR1039517 SRX384354 SRS508576 SAMN02422673 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(counts(dds)) # counts ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SRR1039508 SRR1039509 SRR1039512 SRR1039513 SRR1039516 SRR1039517 TSPAN6 679 448 873 408 1138 1047 DPM1 467 515 621 365 587 799 SCYL3 260 211 263 164 245 331 C1orf112 60 55 40 35 78 63 CFH 3251 3679 6177 4252 6721 11027 FUCA2 1433 1062 1733 881 1424 1439 SRR1039520 SRR1039521 TSPAN6 770 572 DPM1 417 508 SCYL3 233 229 C1orf112 76 60 CFH 5176 7995 FUCA2 1359 1109 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} head(rowData(dds)) # gene_anno ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` DataFrame with 6 rows and 9 columns ensgene entrez symbol chr gene_start gene_end TSPAN6 ENSG00000000003 7105 TSPAN6 X 99883667 99894988 DPM1 ENSG00000000419 8813 DPM1 20 49551404 49575092 SCYL3 ENSG00000000457 57147 SCYL3 1 169818772 169863408 C1orf112 ENSG00000000460 55732 C1orf112 1 169631245 169823221 CFH ENSG00000000971 3075 CFH 1 196621008 196716634 FUCA2 ENSG00000001036 2519 FUCA2 6 143815948 143832827 gene_strand biotype description TSPAN6 -1 protein_coding tetraspanin 6 DPM1 -1 protein_coding dolichyl-phosphate m.. SCYL3 -1 protein_coding SCY1-like 3 (S. cere.. C1orf112 1 protein_coding chromosome 1 open re.. CFH 1 protein_coding complement factor H FUCA2 -1 protein_coding fucosidase, alpha-L-.. ``` ::: ::: ## Running DESeq `DESeq()` this function does the following steps: 1. estimation of size factors - normalization 2. estimation of dispersion 3. Negative Binomial GLM fitting and Wald statistics - prepares for differential expression These steps are basically normalization and preparation for differential expression testing (log2 fold change and p-value) and are almost always run with default parameters. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds <- DESeq(dds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` estimating size factors ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` estimating dispersions ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` gene-wise dispersion estimates ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` mean-dispersion relationship ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` final dispersion estimates ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` fitting model and testing ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} dds ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class: DESeqDataSet dim: 13042 8 metadata(1): version assays(4): counts mu H cooks rownames(13042): TSPAN6 DPM1 ... GTF2H5 NUDT3 rowData names(43): ensgene entrez ... deviance maxCooks colnames(8): SRR1039508 SRR1039509 ... SRR1039520 SRR1039521 colData names(10): SampleName cell ... BioSample sizeFactor ``` ::: ::: You can notice that after running this function, there are new elements added to the dds object: new assays, sizeFactor in colData etc. You can also access normalized counts. Notice how they changed from integers to decimals. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(counts(dds, normalize=TRUE)) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` SRR1039508 SRR1039509 SRR1039512 SRR1039513 SRR1039516 SRR1039517 TSPAN6 667.15192 499.89296 747.77137 609.85899 971.18661 747.93274 DPM1 458.85117 574.65374 531.91984 545.58463 500.95478 570.77198 SCYL3 255.46318 235.44066 225.27362 245.13940 209.08675 236.45247 C1orf112 58.95304 61.37079 34.26215 52.31633 66.56639 45.00455 CFH 3194.27228 4105.14777 5290.93215 6355.68727 5735.80425 7877.22479 FUCA2 1407.99513 1185.01412 1484.40755 1316.87688 1215.26339 1027.96105 SRR1039520 SRR1039521 TSPAN6 841.69621 601.72742 DPM1 455.82769 534.40127 SCYL3 254.69509 240.90136 C1orf112 83.07651 63.11826 CFH 5657.94751 8410.50823 FUCA2 1485.53915 1166.63585 ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # raw counts can still be obtained with # counts(dds, normalize=FALSE) ``` ::: # Principal component analysis After RNA-seq you have a matrix of counts: 13,000 genes (rows) by 8 samples. Each sample is a point in 13,000-dimensional space, which you can't look at. But many genes move together. For example, hundreds of inflammation genes rise and fall as a group. So the data really vary along far fewer independent directions than 13,000. PCA finds new axes, called principal components, that are weighted combinations of genes. PC1 is the single direction along which the samples spread out the most. PC2 is the next-most-variable direction, at right angles to PC1, and so on. Plotting each sample's position on PC1 against PC2 gives a scatterplot. Samples close together have similar overall expression profiles. The axis labels report the percentage of total variance each PC captures, which tells you how much of the full picture the plot actually shows. PCA is a quality-control and exploration step. It is *not* part of the differential expression test itself. You use it to ask a few questions: - Do replicates of the same condition cluster together? - Does PC1 separate your biological groups (treated vs. control), or does it separate something unwanted, like sequencing batch, sex, or the day samples were processed? If batch dominates, you'd add it to your design formula (`~ batch + condition`). - Is there an outlier sample that looks like neither group? PCA requires data transformation that is different that what we did with `DESeq()` function. We need to apply variance-stabilizing transformation, which puts genes on a comparable scale. To do so, we will use `vst()` function. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vsd <- vst(dds, blind=FALSE) ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} vsd ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` class: DESeqTransform dim: 13042 8 metadata(1): version assays(1): '' rownames(13042): TSPAN6 DPM1 ... GTF2H5 NUDT3 rowData names(43): ensgene entrez ... maxCooks dispFit colnames(8): SRR1039508 SRR1039509 ... SRR1039520 SRR1039521 colData names(10): SampleName cell ... BioSample sizeFactor ``` ::: ::: I will show two methods of running PCA: one is built in DESeq2 and is simpler, and another using `PCAtools` package, which I prefer because it gives me more control. 1. DESeq default ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} plotPCA(vsd, intgroup=c("cell", "dex")) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` using ntop=500 top features by variance ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DESeq2_workflow_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-28-1.png){fig-align='center' width=450} ::: ::: There is a message saying `using ntop=500 top features by variance`. Most of the genes are not highly variable across samples (e.g. house keeping genes) and they are not very informative of sample composition and sample-to-sample differences. That's why we use a fraction genes with the highest variance - they are the most informative ones, because they vary the most across samples. `plotPCA` uses top 500 most highly variable genes by default. 2. Using `PCAtools` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} pca_plot <- vsd %>% assay %>% pca(., vsd@colData, removeVar = 0.9) %>% # remove 90% of lower variance -> retains top 10% most variable genes biplot(colby = "cell", shape = 'dex', legendPosition = 'right', lab = NULL ) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` -- removing the lower 90% of variables based on variance ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} pca_plot ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DESeq2_workflow_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-29-1.png){fig-align='center' width=450} ::: ::: Color represents cell line and shape represents treatment status. Thanks to this we can easily identify the main sources of variation: - PC1 explains 50% of variation and is driven by dex (treatment status) - triangles and dots are clearly separated on the X axis. This is great, because it means that the treatment made a real difference - PC2 explains 20% variation and is driven by cell line - different colors separate along the Y axis, with the blue color separating the most from the rest. It is expected to see such spread between biological replicates, because each replicate is a separate cell line. There are differences in baseline expression between different cell lines, which is why we see such separation on PC2. This is also why we included cell line in the design - we don't want the differences between cell lines mask the effect of treatment, especially in a paired design. We can color or shape the plot by every variable that exist in our metadata column. It is a good practice to play with them, because it might help identify sources of technical variability that can be accounted for in the DESeq design. > **Exercise 1** > > Using information available in the metadata table, check whether there are any other factors that can be correlated with PC1 or PC2. > Write a short comment on your observations. # DESeq2 workflow: Part II ## Differential expression test Now that we normalized the data and did a QC check with PCA, we can perform Differential Gene Expression - the clue of the analysis. In DGE we look for differences in gene expression across two different conditions. For example: Gene A is 2x highly expressed in the treated group than untreated. We will use `results()` function that return a table with log2 fold change difference between group 1 and group 2 and a p-value. We need to specify `contrast` which takes a vector of characters: `c(column in metadata, group 1, group 2)`. Here, we want to investigate the effect of dexamethasone treatment, so we will use dex column and compare trt vs. untrt. Alternatively, we can use `name` parameter. The names of coefs can be checked with `resultsNames`. Sometimes, in complex designs, not all comparisons are generated. In that case we can always stick to `contrast` ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} resultsNames(dds) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] "Intercept" "cell_N061011_vs_N052611" [3] "cell_N080611_vs_N052611" "cell_N61311_vs_N052611" [5] "dex_trt_vs_untrt" ``` ::: ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- results(dds, name = "dex_trt_vs_untrt", alpha = 0.05) # alpha is the p-value threshold to whether call a gene significant or not. # alternatively (gives the same numbers, but lfcShrink() cannot be given this res, because it needs the coefficient name) # res <- results(dds, contrast = c("dex", "trt", "untrt"), alpha = 0.05) ``` ::: We can obtain a summary of our results ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} summary(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` out of 13042 with nonzero total read count adjusted p-value < 0.05 LFC > 0 (up) : 2024, 16% LFC < 0 (down) : 1810, 14% outliers [1] : 0, 0% low counts [2] : 0, 0% (mean count < 7) [1] see 'cooksCutoff' argument of ?results [2] see 'independentFiltering' argument of ?results ``` ::: ::: Out of 13055 tested genes 2023 are expressed higher after the treatment than in control (upregulated) and 1810 are expressed lower after the treatment than in the control (downregulated) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} head(res) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` log2 fold change (MLE): dex trt vs untrt Wald test p-value: dex trt vs untrt DataFrame with 6 rows and 6 columns baseMean log2FoldChange lfcSE stat pvalue padj TSPAN6 710.9023 -0.3931219 0.0998230 -3.938189 8.20989e-05 5.62952e-04 DPM1 521.6206 0.1949790 0.1110837 1.755245 7.92175e-02 1.86333e-01 SCYL3 237.8066 0.0260878 0.1411885 0.184773 8.53407e-01 9.17420e-01 C1orf112 58.0835 -0.1010442 0.2817225 -0.358666 7.19845e-01 8.36203e-01 CFH 5828.4405 0.4144951 0.0882133 4.698781 2.61719e-06 2.52627e-05 FUCA2 1286.2116 -0.2529580 0.0884951 -2.858441 4.25728e-03 1.78890e-02 ``` ::: ::: `res` is the main result of the analysis. It has one row per gene and answers the question: "did this gene change after dexamethasone treatment, and by how much?" The columns are: - `baseMean` - average normalized expression of the gene across all samples. Tells you how highly the gene is expressed overall. - `log2FoldChange` - the size and direction of the change (treated vs. untreated). A value of 1 means 2x higher in treated, -1 means 2x lower, 0 means no change. - `lfcSE` - standard error of the log2 fold change, i.e. how uncertain that estimate is. - `stat` - the Wald test statistic (`log2FoldChange / lfcSE`). The p-value is derived from it. - `pvalue` - the probability of seeing a change at least this large if the gene was **not** truly affected by the treatment. - `padj` - the p-value adjusted for multiple testing. **This is the value to use to call genes significant.** ## Adjusted p-value and multiple testing correction A p-value of 0.05 means that there is a 5% chance of getting a result this extreme just by luck, even if nothing is going on. That is fine for one test, but here we test \~13,000 genes at once. If none of the genes were truly changed, we would still expect 0.05 × 13,000 = **\~650 genes** with p \< 0.05 purely by chance. These false positives would be mixed in with the real hits, and we could not tell which are which. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} sum(res$pvalue < 0.05) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 4956 ``` ::: ::: If we hadn't correct the p-value for multiple testing, we would have to expect that 13% of "significant" genes could be actually not significant - false positive **Multiple testing correction** fixes this by making the threshold stricter the more genes we test. DESeq2 uses the Benjamini-Hochberg method, which controls the **false discovery rate (FDR)**. The adjusted p-value (`padj`) is the expected proportion of false positives among the genes called significant at that cutoff. For example, if we keep all genes with `padj` \< 0.05, we accept that about 5% of them may be false positives. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} 0.05 * sum(res$padj < 0.05) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout} ``` [1] 191.7 ``` ::: ::: A useful metric or test to check if our differential expression test was well calibrated and the results are reliable is to look the distribution of nominal (raw) p-values - If the test is well calibrated, genes with no real effect (nulls) have p-values spread evenly between 0 and 1. Genes with a real effect pile up near 0. A healthy histogram is therefore a flat floor with a spike at the left edge. The height of the flat part gives a rough sense of how many genes are truly unchanged.expected, before you trust the padj values. - Uniform shape with no spike: there is little or no signal, or the experiment is underpowered. - Hill-shaped or skewed toward 1: the test is too conservative. This often points to a wrong variance or dispersion estimate, or to a problem in the pre-filtering. - A spike near 0 plus an excess of p-values near 1: the model is probably misspecified, for example a missing batch or covariate in the design. - Strange spikes at specific values: these usually come from low-count genes with discrete p-values. Filtering low-count genes (which the workflow already does) removes most of them. Why it matters. Multiple testing correction, including Benjamini-Hochberg, assumes the null p-values are uniform. If they aren't, padj and the FDR it promises are unreliable, and the list of significant genes may contain many more false positives, or miss many more real ones, than stated. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} p_hist <- ggplot(res, aes(x=pvalue)) + geom_histogram() + theme_bw() p_hist ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DESeq2_workflow_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-36-1.png){fig-align='center' width=270} ::: ::: In our case the histogram looks perfect - our test is well-calibrated. ## LFC shrinking `lfcShrink()` replaces the noisy maximum-likelihood log2 fold changes from `DESeq()` with empirical Bayes estimates pulled toward zero. For genes with low counts or high dispersion, the raw estimates can be large by chance, and shrinkage reduces them in proportion to how little information the gene carries. Genes with strong evidence barely move. It is worth using whenever fold change magnitude matters: volcano and MA plots, ranking genes by LFC (including GSEA inputs), and applying an LFC cutoff. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} res <- lfcShrink(dds, coef = 'dex_trt_vs_untrt', res = res ,type='apeglm') ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` using 'apeglm' for LFC shrinkage. If used in published research, please cite: Zhu, A., Ibrahim, J.G., Love, M.I. (2018) Heavy-tailed prior distributions for sequence count data: removing the noise and preserving large differences. Bioinformatics. https://doi.org/10.1093/bioinformatics/bty895 ``` ::: ::: ## Volcano Plot Volcano plots are a common way to display DGE results. Each point is a gene, with log2 fold change on the x-axis and -log10 adjusted p-value on the y-axis, so genes with large, significant changes sit in the upper corners. DESeq2 doesn't have any built-in volcano plot function. We can use `EnhancedVolcano` package that offers quick plotting functions. I do recommend writing your own custom plotting functions. First of all, you have more control of what is shown and the aesthetics, but it also help you understand the data structure better. Let's test EnhancedVolcano first. ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} EnhancedVolcano(res, lab = rownames(res), x = 'log2FoldChange', y = 'padj', title = 'Dex: trt vs. untrt', subtitle = NULL, pCutoff = 0.05, FCcutoff = 0, pointSize = 1.0) ``` ::: {.cell-output-display} ![](DESeq2_workflow_files/figure-html/unnamed-chunk-38-1.png){fig-align='center' width=450} ::: ::: **Let's create a custom volcano plot** 1. Reading them one by one is not practical. Gene Ontology (GO) helps by grouping genes into labeled sets, such as “inflammatory response” or “cell cycle”, based on what past studies reported about each gene. Enrichment analysis asks whether your gene list contains more genes from a given set than you would expect by chance. Say 5% of all expressed genes belong to “inflammatory response”. If 20% of your upregulated genes do, that term is enriched. The test is usually a hypergeometric (Fisher) test against a background of all genes you could have detected, followed by multiple-testing correction (FDR). **Why we split up and down genes**\ Up and down genes usually reflect different biology. In inflamed gut tissue, for example, upregulated genes tend to hit immune terms, and downregulated genes tend to hit epithelial transport and metabolism. If you pool them, the larger group dominates and the smaller signal gets diluted. Separate analyses are also easier to read, since each result list has a direction. Splitting reduces the number of genes per test, which lowers power, so a weak signal can disappear (see Hong et al. 2014, *J R Soc Interface*, for a comparison of the two approaches). **What a significant term means**\ A significant term means your up (or down) genes contain more members of that term than chance predicts. That is all. It is an association between a gene list and a label. It does not mean the pathway is activated or repressed. Several things can break that inference - GO terms are unordered gene sets, with no direction. “Negative regulation of apoptosis” contains both genes that block cell death and genes that respond to it. - Upregulated inhibitors can mean the pathway is switched on (negative feedback) or switched off. - mRNA level is a proxy. Pathway activity often depends on protein abundance, phosphorylation, or localization, which RNA-seq does not measure. - In bulk tissue, “T cell activation” going up can mean more T cells are present, not that each T cell is more active. Cell composition changes look like pathway changes. - Well-studied genes carry more annotations, so popular terms get enriched more easily. - Many GO terms overlap heavily (parent and child terms). Ten significant terms may be one signal counted ten times. - The result depends on your cutoffs and background. Changing the padj or log2FC threshold, or using all genes instead of expressed genes as background, can change the top terms. **How to use the results**\ Treat enriched terms as hypotheses and a way to generate a story, then test them. Rank-based methods like GSEA avoid hard cutoffs. Activity-inference tools (e.g. PROGENy, decoupleR) estimate pathway or TF activity from target gene behavior. Orthogonal data such as protein levels, perturbation experiments, or single-cell data can confirm that the pathway really changed.\ We will perform overrepresantation test using `clusterProfiler` package, focusing on Gene Ontology: Biological Processes. Make sure to install [org.Hs.eg.db](BiocManager::install(%22org.Hs.eg.db%22)) ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} # Define gene sets # background genes = all tested genes universe <- rownames(deg_table) down_genes <- deg_table[deg_table$diffexpressed == 'DOWN', 'geneid'] ``` ::: ::: {.cell layout-align="center"} ```{.r .cell-code} GO_down <- enrichGO(down_genes, OrgDb = "org.Hs.eg.db", # Human database keyType = "SYMBOL", ont = "BP", universe = universe, qvalueCutoff = 0.05, readable = TRUE) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` 'select()' returned 1:1 mapping between keys and columns ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in bitr(gene, fromType = fromType, toType = "ENTREZID", OrgDb = OrgDb): 6.24% of input gene IDs are fail to map... ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` 'select()' returned 1:many mapping between keys and columns ``` ::: ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stderr} ``` Warning in bitr(gene, fromType = fromType, toType = "ENTREZID", OrgDb = OrgDb): 8.1% of input gene IDs are fail to map... ``` ::: ```{.r .cell-code} # Some GO terms are reduntant. simplify should help remove redundancy but it might be computationally demanding. Sometimes you may wonder, what my filtering step should look like, what should I include in the deseq design, should I apply a log2FC cutoff. And often times the answer is: you need to try different approaches and see which one works best. ## Log2 fold change cutoff The adjusted p-value tells you whether a gene’s change is distinguishable from zero. It says nothing about size. With enough replicates or high counts, a 5% change can be highly significant, and such changes are often too small to matter biologically. A log2FC cutoff keeps only genes with an effect large enough to care about. A common choice is \|log2FC\| \> 1 (2-fold) or and 0.5 is also used.
